passages.where: Jesus tells of a servant forgiven a debt he could never repay, who then throttles a fellow servant over a small one. The master's question is the heart of the story: having been shown that much mercy, should he not have shown a little?

In the same chapter, before Peter's question about how often to forgive, Jesus tells his followers to go to someone who has sinned against them and confront him privately. Forgiveness in the Bible does not mean pretending nothing happened.
Jesus joins two things: rebuke a brother who sins, and forgive him when he repents, as often as he returns. The apostles' answer in the next verse is “Increase our faith!” They knew how hard it was.

Paul describes the clothes of the new life in Christ: compassion, kindness, humility, gentleness and patience. Forgiveness comes in that list, with the Lord's forgiveness as its measure. It belongs to the shared life of a church, where people really do have complaints against each other.

Bitterness, rage and malice are named first, as things that have to be put away. Forgiveness is not a feeling that replaces them by itself. It is a choice made again and again, “just as in Christ God forgave you.”

Paul tells Christians who would suffer real wrongs not to take revenge. He does not say justice does not matter. He says it belongs to God. Letting go of revenge is trust that the wrong will be judged by someone who judges rightly.

After their father dies, Joseph's brothers fear he will finally pay them back for selling him into slavery. Joseph refuses to take God's place. He names what they did as evil, sees God's purpose through it, and promises to provide for them. It had taken years.
Jesus prays for the people crucifying him while they divide his clothes. The prayer is for those doing the harm, spoken while the harm is still being done.
In the prayer Jesus taught, asking God's forgiveness and forgiving others are bound together in one line. A person who prays it is reminded every day of being forgiven.
David praises a God who does not repay sins in kind and removes them as far as the east is from the west. The forgiveness Christians are asked to give flows from the forgiveness they have received.

misread.taken: “Seventy-seven times” is sometimes used to press a person to keep returning to someone who goes on hurting them, as if forgiving meant forgetting, trusting again at once, and accepting more harm.
misread.says: Peter offers seven as a generous limit, and Jesus answers that forgiveness is not to be counted. But the same chapter has just told the wronged person to confront the wrong (Matthew 18:15-17), and Luke's telling joins forgiveness to rebuke and repentance (Luke 17:3-4). Forgiving releases the debt and the right to revenge. It does not erase what happened, it does not mean trust is restored straight away, and it never requires anyone to stay where they or their children are in danger.

whole: Being wronged leaves a mark. A parent who failed you, a spouse who lied, a friend who used your trust, a church that covered a harm. The memory plays again at odd hours. Many people who come to this question have already been told to forgive, quickly and completely, and have been left feeling that their pain is the problem. Others have tried, and found that the anger comes back.

The Bible does not make forgiveness small. It names wrongs as wrongs; Joseph tells his brothers plainly that they meant it for evil. It tells the wronged person to speak to the one who did it. It keeps justice in God's hands and insists he will do it. Forgiveness in Scripture is not saying the debt was nothing. It is cancelling a real debt, the way God cancelled ours, at great cost to himself. That is why it is hard, and why Jesus' disciples answered his teaching with a prayer for more faith.

So forgiveness is usually a decision before it is a feeling, and a road more than a moment. It means giving up the right to get even, again whenever the memory returns. It means praying for the person who hurt you, even through clenched teeth. It does not mean pretending, or reconciling where there is no repentance, or trusting where there is still danger. A person can forgive and still keep a boundary, still report a crime, still grieve. Over time, the hold the wrong has on the heart can loosen. That is God's work as much as ours.

differ.share: Christians agree that God commands his people to forgive, that revenge belongs to God, and that forgiving does not deny that a real wrong was done.

views.name: Forgive from the heart, always
views.body: Some teach that Christians are to forgive from the heart whether or not the wrongdoer ever repents, as Jesus prayed for those crucifying him, while reconciliation waits on repentance.

views.name: Ready to forgive, completed in repentance
views.body: Others hold that full forgiveness, like God's, is given when the wrongdoer repents (Luke 17:3), and that before then the Christian's duty is to give up bitterness and revenge and to stand ready to forgive.

differ.after: Both refuse revenge and bitterness, and both distinguish forgiving from trusting again.

sit: What would it mean to hand this wrong to God to judge, without telling him or yourself that it did not matter?

prayer.lead: Psalm 62 tells a person to pour out their heart before God. Begin there, with the whole of it.
